content: The development of these guidelines was led by Dr. Philippa Easterbrook from the Department of HIV/AIDS in Switzerland and Dr. Elizabeth Mason from the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health in Switzerland. They were supported in the initial stages by Mike Zangenberg, also from the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health. Additional contributions were made by WHO staff, including Frank Lule (HIV/AIDS, Regional Office for Africa, Brazzaville), Kasonde Mwinga (Maternal and Child Health, Regional Office for Africa, Brazzaville), Meg Doherty (Department of HIV/AIDS, Switzerland), Rajiv Bahl (Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, Switzerland), Wilson Were (Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health, Switzerland), and Poul Erik Petersen (Department of Chronic Diseases and Health Promotion/Oral Health Unit, Switzerland). Peggy Henderson, a consultant, prepared the initial drafts of the guidelines and conducted the final editing. Dr. Philippa Easterbrook authored the section on Kaposi sarcoma, while John Stephen provided technical inputs to the draft. Nadia Pillai, Stephanie Sharabianlou, and Elizabeth Centeno Tablante supported the WHO in drafting the guidelines as interns and volunteers, respectively. The development of this publication was funded by a grant from the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The CDC also provided support by releasing Dr. Mamadou O. Diallo for the technical preparation of the Guidelines Development Group meeting. Dr. Diallo contributed in his individual capacity during this time. WHO expressed gratitude to the institutions that contributed staff time and other in-kind resources to the guidelines development process. The International Federation of Dermatology, which receives some funding from industry for specific projects, did not contribute commercial funding to the development of these guidelines. Despite the increasing availability of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens, HIV-associated opportunistic infections (OIs) continue to cause significant morbidity and mortality, particularly in resource-limited settings where treatment coverage remains low and diagnoses are often made at advanced stages of disease. Poor management standards for OIs and co-morbidities, as well as limited access to OI drugs, contribute to high HIV-related mortality in these settings. Global guidance on the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of major OIs and co-morbidities in adults and children has been lacking, prompting many countries to request such guidelines. In response, the WHO’s Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health (MCA), in collaboration with the Department of HIV/AIDS, developed these guidelines to address common skin and oral conditions associated with HIV. The primary objectives of these guidelines are to summarize key evidence and provide practice recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of major skin and oral conditions in HIV-infected adults and children. The target audience includes healthcare professionals responsible for providing care to children, adolescents, and adults in resource-limited settings with HIV. Additionally, policymakers, managers of HIV/AIDS and disease control programs, health facilities, and teaching institutions are expected to use these guidelines to establish and maintain care services. The guidelines describe common HIV-related dermatologic and oral conditions in resource-limited settings, their differential diagnoses, and treatment strategies likely to be locally available. An algorithmic tool is being developed by a multi-agency group led by WHO to assist clinicians in diagnosing HIV-related dermatologic conditions based on expert opinion. The development and review of these guidelines followed the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. A systematic review addressing population, intervention, comparator, and outcomes (PICO) questions was conducted for each condition, with search strategies and inclusion criteria detailed. A final consensus meeting of the Guidelines Development Group (GDG) was held in Geneva from September 25–27, 2013, where evidence, assessments, and evaluations were reviewed, revisions were suggested, and final recommendations were approved. Further refinements were made through electronic communications and teleconferences, and a peer review group provided comments on a draft document. The final recommendations were submitted for approval by the WHO Guidelines Review Committee. The guidelines address conditions such as Kaposi sarcoma, seborrheic dermatitis, papular pruritic eruption, eosinophilic folliculitis, tinea infections, herpes zoster, scabies, molluscum contagiosum, oropharyngeal candidiasis, and Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis. For each condition, specific treatment recommendations and evidence summaries are provided, along with considerations for implementation. For Kaposi sarcoma, immediate ART initiation is recommended for mild/moderate disease, while severe/symptomatic cases require ART combined with systemic chemotherapy. Recommended chemotherapy regimens include vincristine with bleomycin and doxorubicin (ABV), bleomycin with vincristine (BV), liposomal anthracyclines, paclitaxel, or oral etoposide, depending on local resources and infrastructure. For seborrheic dermatitis, topical ketoconazole 2% is recommended for mild cases, with maintenance treatment as needed. Severe cases should prompt HIV testing, and if positive, ART initiation should be assessed. For papular pruritic eruption, ART is the primary treatment, with topical corticosteroids recommended for persistent symptoms. For eosinophilic folliculitis, ART is the primary treatment, and patients should not discontinue ART if the condition develops after initiation. Topical corticosteroids, oral itraconazole, or permethrin 5% cream may be added if symptoms persist. For tinea infections, topical treatments such as terbinafine 1% or miconazole are recommended for non-extensive cases. If there is no response, oral terbinafine or itraconazole should be used. HIV testing is recommended for patients with unknown HIV status. For herpes zoster, acyclovir is recommended to prevent disease dissemination and resolve symptoms. HIV testing should be offered to patients with unknown HIV status. For scabies, topical permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate is recommended for mild/moderate cases. Oral ivermectin is recommended for poor treatment response or severe/crusted scabies in patients weighing ≥15 kg. For children <15 kg, topical permethrin or benzyl benzoate should be used, with keratolytics like 5% salicylic acid to remove scale bulk. For molluscum contagiosum, ART is the primary treatment for extensive or unusually distributed cases. HIV testing is recommended for new-onset cases in high HIV-prevalence settings. For oropharyngeal candidiasis, oral fluconazole is the preferred treatment for adults and children. Topical therapies like nystatin or clotrimazole are alternatives when fluconazole is unavailable. Prompt ART initiation is recommended for all HIV-infected patients with oropharyngeal candidiasis. For Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis, specific recommendations for HIV-infected children and adults are provided in the guidelines.
